title: What Information Matters? Graph Out-of-Distribution Detection via Tri-Component Information Decomposition
claim: Prior methods keep mixed or spurious input-specific information; ours decomposes it and isolates only the joint label-relevant component.
layout: 2 Venn panels side by side, left-to-right, legend at left, arrows extracting components
description: Two three-circle Venn diagrams are placed side by side, joined by a thick black arrow. Each diagram has circles for Label Y on top and node features X and graph structure A at the bottom. A legend at the far left explains the patterns: pink grid for GIB representation, grey vertical hatching for irrelevant information, grid plus hatching for overfitting, a dashed red oval for the SL representation, and a red-outlined blue triangle for the Tide representation. In the left panel (GIB), a pink gridded region overlaps Y, X and A, and a dashed red ellipse marks the SL representation. In the right panel (Tide), the Y overlap is split into three parts. The green part is feature-specific, labeled I(X;Y|Z). The orange part is structure-specific, labeled I(A;Y|Z). The blue part is the joint region, labeled I(Z;Y), and it is outlined with a red triangle. Colored arrows point outward from the green and orange parts, and a blue arrow points out from the joint part. The eye goes first to the colorful right-hand Venn diagram.
caption: Comparison of information captured by standard supervised learning (SL), GIB [ref], and Tide. The dashed red circle shows that SL mixes label-relevant and irrelevant feature and structure signals, causing spurious correlations that make OOD nodes appear ID. The gridded region indicates that GIB suppresses label-irrelevant noise but still keeps input-specific spurious cues. Contrary, Tide (solid red triangle) isolates the joint label-relevant information by decomposing spurious feature-/structure-specific components, thereby improving OOD detection.
abstract: Graph neural networks are widely used for node classification, but they remain vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts in node features and graph structure. Prior work established that methods trained with standard supervised learning (SL) objectives tend to capture spurious signals from either features and/or structure, leaving the model fragile under distributional changes. To address this, we propose TIDE, a novel and effective Tri-Component Information Decomposition framework that explicitly decomposes information into feature-specific, structure-specific and joint components. TIDE aims to preserve only the label-relevant part of the joint information while filtering out spurious feature- and structure-specific information, thereby enhancing the separation between in-distribution (ID) and OOD nodes. Beyond the framework, we provide theoretical and empirical analyses showing that an information bottleneck objective is preferable to standard SL for graph OOD detection, with higher ID confidence and a greater entropy gap between ID and OOD data. Extensive experiments across seven datasets confirm the efficacy of TIDE, achieving up to a 34% improvement in FPR95 over strong baselines while maintaining competitive ID accuracy.
